Below is a comprehensive roadmap that outlines how to reproduce the experiments and methods described in the paper. This plan is designed to help you write the eventual Python code and set up a reproducible experimental pipeline. Some details (such as the exact architectural choices for the Transformer and ResNet backbones) must be adapted from the referenced work [13], and there is slight ambiguity in the precise form of Equation 2 (the periodic activation) that you should decide on based on best practices (e.g. using sin/cos functions). In any case, the following plan captures all the major details:

──────────────────────────────
1. OVERVIEW & KEY IDEAS

• The paper argues that embeddings for numerical features are an underexplored degree of freedom in tabular deep learning.  
• Two main embedding strategies are proposed:
  – Piecewise Linear Encoding (PLE) with two variants:
    ∙ Quantile-based PLE: uses empirical quantiles to obtain split boundaries.
    ∙ Target-aware (tree-based) PLE: uses supervised discretization (similar to C4.5) per feature.
  – Periodic Embeddings: Use periodic (sinusoidal) activations with trainable pre-activation coefficients (initialized with N(0, σ)) and a tunable multiplier “k”.  
• The embeddings are then fed into different backbones (MLP, ResNet, Transformer) using a “Backbone-Embedding” pattern. For MLP-style models, feature embeddings are computed independently and then concatenated, while for Transformer-like models these tokenized embeddings are passed without extra mixing except that an additional linear layer may be applied to inject feature index information.

──────────────────────────────
2. METHODOLOGY – IMPLEMENTING THE EMBEDDING MODULES

A. Baseline / Simple Differentiable Embeddings  
  • Implement a simple linear layer (optionally with ReLU or LeakyReLU) on each numerical feature.  
  • This “LR” module acts as a baseline.

B. Piecewise Linear Encoding (PLE) Module  
  • Compute bins for each numeric feature (each feature is processed independently):  
   – Quantile Approach:  
    ▪ Use the training set to compute empirical quantiles.
    ▪ Remove any trivial (zero-width) bins.
    ▪ Hyperparameter: number of quantiles (search space UniformInt[2, 256]).  
   – Target-Aware (Tree-Based) Approach:  
    ▪ Fit a one-dimensional decision tree on each feature using the target as guidance.
    ▪ Use parameters similar to “C4.5 discretization”:
     – Maximum number of leaves (UniformInt[2,256]),
     – Minimum samples per leaf (UniformInt[1,128]), and
     – Minimum information gain (LogUniform[1e-9, 0.01]).
  • For each scalar value x, create the PLE encoding vector e = [e₁, …, e_T] according to Equation 1:
   – e_t = 0 if x is below the (t–1)th bin boundary (with t > 1);
   – e_t = 1 if x is above or equal to the t-th bin boundary (with t < T);
   – Otherwise, compute a linear interpolation: (x – bₜ₋₁) / (bₜ – bₜ₋₁).
  • The final feature embedding is given by a trainable linear combination:
    fᵢ(x) = v₀ + Σₜ eₜ · vₜ  
    – Here, v₀ and vₜ are learnable parameters (embedding vectors) for that feature.
  • Optionally, experiment with additional differentiable layers on top of the PLE output (e.g., adding an extra linear or ReLU block).

C. Periodic Embedding Module  
  • For each numerical feature, implement a transformation that uses periodic activations:
   – Example formulation: fᵢ(x) = Linear( sin( k · x + cᵢ ) )  
    – k is a tunable hyperparameter (UniformInt[1, 128]).
    – cᵢ is a trainable parameter for each feature (initialize via N(0, σ) where σ is tuned).
  • Like in the PLE modules, the result can optionally be enhanced by stacking an extra differentiable (e.g., linear) layer that “wraps” the periodic module.
  • Note: The paper’s Equation 2 is brief; you need to choose a periodic function (sin, cosine, or both) and then add the additional linear transformation as suggested.

──────────────────────────────
3. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP

A. Datasets & Preprocessing  
  • Use eleven public tabular datasets (as described):
   – Gesture Phase Prediction
   – Churn Modelling (e.g., from Kaggle)
   – California Housing
   – House 16H
   – Adult (income estimation)
   – Otto Group Product Classification
   – Higgs
   – Santander Customer Transaction Prediction
   – Facebook Comments
   – Covertype
   – Microsoft/MSLR-WEB10K (treat ranking as regression)
  • Synthetic GBDT-Friendly Dataset:
   – 10,000 samples, 8 features (sampled from N(0, 1))
   – Target is generated using 16 decision trees of depth 6.
  • Preprocessing:  
   – For all datasets except Otto, apply quantile transformation (scikit-learn’s QuantileTransformer) on numeric features.
   – Standardize regression targets.
   – For categorical features (in non–tree-based models), use one-hot encoding (CatBoost has inbuilt support).
  • Data Splits:  
   – Split the dataset into training, validation, and test sets
   – The training set is used to compute quantiles (or train the decision tree for target-aware bins) and learn model parameters.
   – Use the validation set for early stopping and hyperparameter tuning.
   – Use the test set strictly for reporting final performance.
  • Batch Sizes: Choose predefined values per dataset (details in Appendix C of the paper).

B. Backbones  
  • Implement three types of backbones:
   1. MLP  
    – An MLP of four layers (e.g., 256 units per layer) is mentioned for the synthetic data.
    – The embeddings for each numeric feature are concatenated.
   2. ResNet  
    – Incorporates residual connections; refer to prior work [13] for specific architecture details.
   3. Transformer (FT-Transformer)  
    – The tokenized embeddings are used directly, and if necessary, a dedicated linear layer is added to inject feature-index information.
  • For each backbone, allow the “embedding module” to be swapped (baseline linear, PLE variants, periodic).

C. Training Details  
  • Loss Functions:  
   – Use cross-entropy for classification problems.
   – Use mean squared error (MSE) for regression.
  • Optimizer: Use AdamW for all models.
  • Learning Rate: Tune via hyperparameter search; use log-uniform distributions as suggested.
  • Early Stopping:  
   – Monitor validation performance.
   – Patience = 16 epochs (stop training after 16+1 epochs with no improvement).
  • Repeat each experiment with 15 different random seeds to get reliable mean and standard deviation statistics.

D. Hyperparameter Tuning  
  • Use Optuna with the Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) algorithm.  
  • Define search spaces:  
   – Output dimensions of linear layers (UniformInt[1, 128]).  
   – For quantile-based PLE: number of quantiles (UniformInt[2, 256]).  
   – For tree-based PLE: max number of leaves (UniformInt[2,256]), minimum items per leaf (UniformInt[1,128]), minimum information gain (LogUniform[1e-9, 0.01]).  
   – For the periodic module: k (UniformInt[1,128]) and initialization σ for cᵢ (value to be tuned).  
   – Backbone-specific parameters: number of layers, hidden unit sizes, dropout rates, learning rate (log-uniform), weight decay, etc.
  • Tune based on the performance on the validation set; do not access the test set during tuning.

E. Evaluation Metrics  
  • Classification tasks: Report accuracy (Acc.)  
  • Regression tasks: Report root-mean-square error (RMSE)  
  • For each configuration, report average performance and standard deviations over 15 random seeds.
  • Also, evaluate ensemble predictions by splitting the 15 individual runs into three disjoint groups and averaging (similar to what is done in Table 6).

──────────────────────────────
4. CODE STRUCTURE & IMPLEMENTATION ROADMAP

A. Environment Setup  
  • Use a deep learning framework (PyTorch or TensorFlow).  
  • Python libraries required: NumPy, Pandas, scikit-learn, Optuna, and logging libraries.  
  • Ensure reproducibility via fixed random seeds and logging of versions.

B. Modules & Components Outline

I. Data Processing Module  
  1. Dataset Loader:  
   – Implement functions to download/load each dataset.
   – Split data into train/validation/test sets.
  2. Preprocessing:  
   – Apply quantile transformation (sklearn’s QuantileTransformer) for numeric features.
   – Standardize regression targets.
   – One-hot encode categorical variables (unless using CatBoost).

II. Embedding Modules  
  1. Baseline Embedding:  
   – A simple linear mapping possibly wrapped with an activation function.
  2. Piecewise Linear Encoding (PLE):  
   – Create a PLE class that, during initialization with training data, computes bin boundaries for each numeric feature using:
    a. Quantile-based method or
    b. Decision tree (target-aware method) as a one-dimensional discretizer.
   – In the forward pass, for an input x, compute the vector of “bin activations” (using zero, one, or linear interpolation as per Equation 1).
   – Multiply the resulting vector by learnable embedding weights (v₀ and vₜ) to get fᵢ(x).
  3. Periodic Embedding:  
   – Implement a module that, for each feature, computes:  
    x → (k * x + cᵢ) → periodic function (e.g., sin()) → Optional linear layer.
   – cᵢ is trainable and initialized from N(0,σ); k is a tunable multiplier.
   – Allow stacking an extra linear layer after the periodic activation.
  4. Combination Options:  
   – Allow combining the embedding module with additional differentiable layers (e.g., “LRLR” or “PLRLR” as in the paper) to balance complexity and efficiency.

III. Backbone Model Implementations  
  1. MLP:  
   – Standard fully connected network that takes concatenated embeddings.
   – Make architecture configurable (number of layers, hidden sizes, dropout).
  2. ResNet:  
   – Implement residual blocks with skip connections.
   – Follow the guidelines or adapt from related literature (reference [13]).
  3. Transformer (FT-Transformer):  
   – Treat each numeric feature’s embedding as a token.
   – Optionally add a linear layer to fuse feature-index information.
   – Follow the hyperparameter suggestions or replicate from [13].

IV. Training Loop & Evaluation  
  1. Write a generic training loop that:  
   – Accepts a model, optimizer (AdamW), and appropriate loss function.
   – Monitors training and validation performance per epoch.
   – Implements early stopping using the patience criteria (e.g. 16 epochs without improvement).
   – Logs the results per epoch.
  2. Validation & Test Evaluation:  
   – At the end of training, evaluate on the test set and record metrics.
   – For each configuration, run 15 experiments with different random seeds.
  3. Ensemble Implementation:  
   – Group the 15 runs (e.g., into three groups) and average predictions to produce ensemble outputs.
   – Compare ensemble performance to individual runs.

V. Hyperparameter Tuning Module  
  1. Set up Optuna studies for:  
   – Backbone-specific parameters (layers, sizes, dropouts, learning rates).
   – Embedding module parameters (number of bins, decision tree splitting hyperparameters, k, σ, and output dimensions).
  2. Define search spaces exactly as described, and run tuning using the validation set.
  3. Log and save the best configuration for each model variant.

VI. Logging & Reproducibility  
  • Log every run along with the random seed, hyperparameters, training curves, and evaluation metrics.  
  • Save model checkpoints, especially the best-performing configuration on validation.  
  • Document library versions and ensure reproducible data splits.

──────────────────────────────
5. EXPERIMENT SCHEDULING & REPORTING

A. Single-model experiments:  
  – Train each model variant (e.g., MLP, MLP-LR, MLP-Q-LR, MLP-T-LR, MLP-P, MLP-PLR, etc.) on every dataset.  
  – Evaluate using 15 random seeds and report mean ± standard deviation.

B. Ensemble experiments:  
  – Form ensembles from the 15 runs as per paper’s protocol.
  – Compare aggregate performance against baseline GBDT models (CatBoost, XGBoost).

C. Ablation Studies:  
  – Compare the effect of different embedding choices (e.g., piecewise linear vs. binary vs. one-blob variants) following Table 8 and Table 9 in the paper.
  – Study sensitivity to preprocessing (vanilla MLP vs. MLP with PLE, with and without quantile transformations).

D. Synthetic Dataset Experiment:  
  – Recreate the synthetic GBDT-friendly dataset as described in section D.1.
  – Experiment with varying the number of bins in the quantile-based PLE and plot RMSE vs. number of bins (cf. Figure 5).

E. Result Reporting  
  – Prepare tables similar to Tables 3–6 that summarize performance metrics.  
  – Plot training curves and performance vs. hyperparameter plots (e.g., effect of number of bins).

──────────────────────────────
6. AMBIGUITIES & DECISION POINTS

• The exact formulation of Equation 2 (for periodic embeddings) is not fully spelt out. Decide on a function such as:  
  fᵢ(x) = Linear( sin(k · x + cᵢ) )  
or use a composite function (e.g., use both sine and cosine concatenated) if that better reflects the intended expressivity.  
• The backbone architectures (especially ResNet and Transformer) are referenced from [13]. If the full details are not available, approximate these architectures based on published details or prior implementations.  
• Details such as exact batch sizes for each dataset are provided in Appendix C of the paper. If not available, choose reasonable defaults and document any differences.

──────────────────────────────
7. SUMMARY

Your roadmap is broken into five major components:
 1. Data preparation and preprocessing.  
 2. Implementation of various embedding modules (baseline, PLE with quantile/target-aware binning, and periodic embeddings).  
 3. Building backbone architectures (MLP, ResNet, Transformer) that accept these embeddings.  
 4. Designing the training loop, hyperparameter tuning using Optuna, and evaluation protocols (including 15-seed runs and ensemble formation).  
 5. Reporting results and performing ablations to compare with GBDT baselines.

By following this detailed plan, you will be able to structure your implementation, replicate the experiments, and eventually compare the empirical performance of the proposed embedding schemes with standard approaches.

This roadmap should give you a strong foundation before writing any final code.
